newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: 11 judges elected to Yugoslav war crimes tribunal.
newsitem.headline: 11 judges elected to Yugoslav war crimes tribunal.

text.p: The General Assembly elected 11 judges on Tuesday to serve four-year terms on the U.N. war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, beginning November 17.
The tribunal, based at The Hague, was established by the Security Council in 1993. The terms of its original 11 judges expire in November.
The Security Council last month nominated 19 candidates. The final choice was up to the Assembly, where an absolute majority of 94 votes was needed to win election.
The following nine jurists were elected on the first round of Assembly ballotting:

Antonio Cassese of Italy, the tribunal's current president (146 votes); Richard May of Britain (129); Mohamed Shahabuddeen of Guyana (127); Wang Tieya of China (123); Claude Jorda of France (119); Gabrielle Kirk McDonald of the United States (118); Fouad Abdel-Moneim Riad of Egypt (118); Lal Chand Vohrah of Malaysia (113); and Rafael Nieto Navia of Colombia (96).
No one received the required majority on the second, third and fifth rounds, and the names of several candidates were withdrawn as the ballotting continued.
Florence Ndepele Mwachande Mumba of Zambia was elected on the fourth round, with 95 votes, and Almiro Simoes Rodrigues of Portugal on the sixth round, with 108 votes.
Five of those elected are currently serving on the court -- Cassese, Jorda, McDonald, Riad and Vohrah.
The tribunal is the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held in the aftermath of World War Two.
It has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.

The first full-length trial ended earlier this month when Dusan "Dusko" Tadic, a Bosnian Serb police reservist, was found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity for his part in a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Bosnian Moslems in 1992. He awaits sentencing. The tribunal cannot impose death sentences.
A Bosnian Croat, Drazen Erdemovic, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail after confessing to killing unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
Six more men are in custody in the tribunal's detention centre awaiting trial.
The two most prominent indicted suspects, who are both at large, are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander General Ratko Mladic.
